cards.title: Permanent lower bounds from black-box identity testing
cards.formal:
Does the following implication hold over the rational field \(\mathbb Q\)?
\[
\mathsf{HIT}_{\mathbb Q}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{PERMHard}_{\mathbb Q}.
\]
The premise \(\mathsf{HIT}_{\mathbb Q}\) says that there are a single deterministic algorithm \(G\) and positive integers \(A,a\) such that, for every \(n,d,s\ge1\), on unary input \((1^{n},1^{d},1^{s})\), algorithm \(G\) outputs a finite list \(H_{n,d,s}\) of points in \(\mathbb Q^{n}\) within \(A(n+d+s)^{a}\) bit operations, with the property
\[
\forall f\in\mathbb Q[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}],\quad
\bigl(f\ne0\ \land\ \deg f\le d\ \land\ L_{\mathbb Q}(f)\le s\bigr)
\ \Longrightarrow\
\exists h\in H_{n,d,s},\quad f(h)\ne0.
\]
Here \(L_{\mathbb Q}(f)\) is the minimum number of edges in a division-free arithmetic circuit over \(\mathbb Q\) computing \(f\), in the model below; rational constants of arbitrary bit length are allowed in those circuits.

The conclusion \(\mathsf{PERMHard}_{\mathbb Q}\) says that the permanent polynomial family has no polynomial-size circuits in that same algebraic model. Explicitly, with
\[
\operatorname{Perm}_{m}(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}x_{i,\pi(i)},
\]
the conclusion is
\[
\forall B,b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall m_{0}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\
\exists m\ge m_{0},\qquad
L_{\mathbb Q}(\operatorname{Perm}_{m})>Bm^{b}.
\]
Prove this implication or its logical negation. The source asks a more general question about circuit classes; this card selects its explicitly published general-circuit black-box instance and fixes the rational field and bit-cost convention as disclosed below.
cards.why: This question asks whether derandomizing algebraic identity testing forces hardness for the permanent, a canonical polynomial encoding counting, rather than merely for less explicitly describable polynomials. A resolution would clarify the strength of the connection between algorithms for detecting algebraic cancellation and nonuniform arithmetic lower bounds, a central barrier in algebraic complexity.

progress.text: The survey’s Theorem 4.6 connects deterministic black-box PIT with circuit lower bounds for a polynomial whose coefficients are computable in polynomial space; the discussion immediately before Open Problem 17 identifies the missing guarantee that the hard polynomial belongs to Valiant’s class \(\mathrm{VNP}\), which would yield permanent hardness.

Aaronson and van Melkebeek sharpen the Boolean alternative in the Kabanets–Impagliazzo disjunction from \(\mathrm{NEXP}\) to \(\mathrm{NEXP}\cap\mathrm{coNEXP}\). Their Corollary 4.2 still has a disjunctive conclusion, and their arithmetic circuits over the integers have only constants zero and one with subtraction allowed.

Jansen and Santhanam obtain permanent lower bounds from specially encoded hitting sets for high-degree univariate polynomials. The hypothesis imposes uniform constant-depth threshold-circuit encodings, and the extension from constant-free to arbitrary-constant arithmetic circuits additionally assumes the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis; this is a different premise from polynomial bit-time generation with a degree parameter.

Carmosino, Impagliazzo, Kabanets and Kolokolova obtain purely arithmetic lower-bound formulations using multilinear polynomial families definable in nondeterministic exponential time and robust simulation notions. Their integer-case equivalence in Theorem 4 does not place the hard family in \(\mathrm{VNP}\) or establish a lower bound for the permanent.

Question 3.2 of Kumar and Saptharishi explicitly asks whether polynomial-time deterministic black-box PIT implies \(\mathrm{VP}\ne\mathrm{VNP}\), citing Open Problem 17 of Shpilka and Yehudayoff. This is the source-posed instance selected here; the rational-field and bit-model details are made explicit in the card.

Andrews, Kush and Tell relate polynomial-time PIT to lower bounds for uniform arithmetic networks, including networks with PIT gates. Their discussion after Theorems 1.2–1.3 explicitly distinguishes these results from nonuniform circuit lower bounds; they do not give the permanent conclusion required here.

Guo’s preprint removes a squarefreeness assumption from deterministic black-box PIT for depth-four circuits with top fan-in three and constant bottom fan-in. This restricted-class result does not settle the general-circuit implication.

sentences: A hitting set is a list of inputs on which every nonzero polynomial in a specified circuit class has a nonzero value somewhere.
The card asks whether a uniform polynomial-time generator of such sets for general rational arithmetic circuits forces the permanent to require more than polynomially many arithmetic edges.
Both sides allow arbitrary rational constants in the circuits, while the generator must write its rational points within a polynomial bit-time bound on unary variable, degree and size parameters.
The published question isolates a missing permanent lower bound beyond established consequences involving other hard polynomials or a disjunction with Boolean circuit hardness.
The general-circuit black-box instance is explicitly sourced, its field and encoding conventions are disclosed, and the bounded review found no later result meeting the full implication.

cards.definitions:
A circuit has a finite directed acyclic graph, a single designated output gate, and commuting variables. Each input gate is labeled by one of the allowed variables or by an arbitrary rational number. Each other gate has two ordered incoming edge slots and is labeled by addition or multiplication. Both slots may refer to the same predecessor, and edges count with multiplicity. Values may be reused at arbitrarily many gates. Only gates lying on a path to the output need be retained. The polynomial at an input gate is its label; the other gates compute the sum or product of their predecessors. Equality is equality of formal polynomials, not agreement on a selected finite set. Division gates, tests, branching and approximation are not allowed. A negative rational constant is allowed, so subtraction needs no extra primitive. The algebraic size is the number of edges, independently of the bit lengths of rational labels. The minimum defining \(L_{\mathbb Q}\) is over all such circuits, with no uniformity requirement.

For an \(n\)-variable polynomial, the circuit may use any subset of \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\). Total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient, with the zero polynomial assigned degree zero for this statement. The bound \(d\) applies to the polynomial at the output; no syntactic-degree bound or bound on intermediate degrees is imposed. The parameter \(s\) is an algebraic edge bound, not a bit-length bound on a circuit encoding. Thus the hitting-set requirement covers circuits with arbitrary rational constants, including constants whose binary encodings are longer than \(s\). A circuit is not supplied to \(G\): the output list depends only on \(n,d,s\), and must work simultaneously for every polynomial satisfying the displayed conditions. Repeated points in the list are harmless.

To fix the bit model, \(G\) is an ordinary deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite alphabet, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes, a read-only input tape and an output tape. One transition reads or writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The input word is \(1^{n}\#1^{d}\#1^{s}\). All transitions, integer and rational arithmetic, memory access and output writing are charged; there are no random bits, advice, oracles or uncharged preprocessing. A fixed finite alphabet changes the bit cost only by a constant factor.

Each rational coordinate in the output is represented uniquely by a sign followed by the binary magnitude of its numerator, a slash, and its positive binary denominator. Numerator and denominator are coprime, there are no leading zeros, and zero is represented as \(+0/1\). Coordinates within a point are separated by commas, and points by semicolons, with no trailing separators; the empty word denotes the empty list. Every point must contain exactly \(n\) coordinates. The output is the explicit list, not a circuit or an oracle for its entries. The running-time bound therefore also bounds its total encoding length, the number of points and their coordinate bit lengths by a fixed polynomial in \(n+d+s\). The machine must halt and satisfy that bound on every valid unary input; no promise about other inputs is needed.

The hitting property is the precise black-box testing premise used here. It asserts an efficiently generated universal set of evaluation points. It does not grant a procedure that can inspect the circuit description, and it does not charge arbitrary-size rational evaluations as unit-cost Boolean operations. The premise is stated directly as a hitting-set construction so that field-operation cost and the bit cost of circuit evaluation are not conflated. Dependence polynomial in \(d\) is permitted; there is no requirement polynomial in \(\log d\).

In the permanent definition, \(S_{m}\) is the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and \(X=(x_{i,j})_{1\le i,j\le m}\) consists of \(m^{2}\) independent commuting variables. The conclusion concerns exact computation of this formal polynomial for all rational assignments. Different matrix dimensions may use unrelated circuits and unrelated rational constants, with no algorithm required to print those circuits. The constants \(B,b\) in a putative polynomial upper bound must be independent of \(m\). The displayed hardness condition means infinitely many violations of each fixed polynomial bound; it does not impose an additional almost-everywhere lower-bound rate. It is equivalent to the absence of constants \(B,b\) for which every \(\operatorname{Perm}_{m}\) has size at most \(Bm^{b}\), since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed by increasing \(B\).

The implication is the sole mathematical target. Its premise is the existence of one uniform hitting-set generator with fixed constants before all three parameters, and its conclusion is a nonuniform arithmetic size lower bound with no restriction on constant bit lengths. Choosing \(\mathbb Q\), specifying bit-time generation, output encoding and output-degree bounds are explicit refinements of the source question, which is stated in algebraic-complexity terminology over characteristic-zero fields.
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\(\mathsf{HIT}_{\mathbb Q}\Rightarrow\mathsf{PERMHard}_{\mathbb Q}\)
or of its logical negation, with all the circuits, encodings, machine resources and quantifiers defined above.

For a positive answer, the theorem must derive the displayed permanent lower bound from precisely the hitting-set existence premise, with no additional hardness, complexity-class, number-theoretic, constant-bit-length or uniformity assumption. The premise is an assumption of the theorem, not an additional construction task that must be solved unconditionally.

For a negative answer, prove \(\mathsf{HIT}_{\mathbb Q}\) together with \(\neg\mathsf{PERMHard}_{\mathbb Q}\). Equivalently, provide the generator \(G\), its constants \(A,a\) and their complete uniform correctness and runtime proof, together with constants \(B,b\ge1\) and a nonuniform family \((C_{m})_{m\ge1}\) of the specified circuits such that
\[
\forall m\ge1,\qquad |C_{m}|\le Bm^{b}
\quad\text{and}\quad C_{m}(X)=\operatorname{Perm}_{m}(X).
\]
Here \(|C_{m}|\) counts edges, and circuit equality is formal polynomial equality. A generator for only a restricted circuit class, a lower bound for some other polynomial family, a Boolean-or-arithmetic disjunction, a bound against only uniform or constant-free circuits, or a relativized obstruction to a particular proof method does not establish either answer for this implication. There is no numerical tolerance in this yes-or-no target.

cards.title: Cubic min-plus circuit lower bounds for shortest paths
cards.formal: For \(n \ge  2\), assign an arbitrary nonnegative real weight \(x_{ij}\) to every unordered edge \(\{i,j\}\) of the complete undirected graph on vertices 1,...,n. Define $f_n(x)=\min_{P:1\leadsto n}\sum_{e\in P}x_e$, where P ranges over simple paths. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input gates \(x_{ij}\) and optional constants 0 and infinity, binary gates \(\min (a,b)\) or \(a+b\), unrestricted reuse of gate outputs, and one designated output. Its topology depends on n but not on x, and it must compute \(f_{n}\) exactly for every permitted weight assignment. Let \(s(n)\) be the minimum number of binary gates in such a circuit. Is \(s(n)=Omega(n^{3})\)? Equivalently, do there exist constants \(c>0\) and n0 such that every such circuit has at least \(c n^{3}\) gates for every \(n\ge n0\)?
cards.definitions: A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences \(x_{ij}\) and \(x_{ji}\) denote the same input, because the graph is undirected. Infinity is an optional internal constant with min(a,infinity)=a and a+infinity=infinity; all input edge weights are finite and nonnegative. The circuit has no subtraction, tests with separate Boolean outputs, conditional routing, or input-dependent memory access. A min gate directly returns the smaller of its two numerical arguments. Input gates, wires, and reuse of an already computed value are free; binary arithmetic gates are counted. Circuits need not be generated uniformly by an efficient algorithm, so the proposed lower bound is nonuniform and imposes no depth restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified cubic lower bound, or refute it by proving its negation: for every \(c>0\) and every n0 there is an \(n\ge n0\) with a correct circuit using fewer than \(c n^{3}\) gates. An \(o(n^{3})\)-size circuit family for all sufficiently large n would suffice for a negative answer. A lower bound for a more restricted circuit class, for all-pairs output, or for shortest paths allowing negative input weights does not establish this statement.
cards.why: This is a basic unconditional lower-bound question for dynamic programming. A resolution would clarify whether the standard cubic relaxation computation is intrinsically necessary even for one distance when computation is restricted to minimum and addition, and would illuminate why monotone lower-bound methods struggle with paths of varying lengths.

importance.reason: A central explicit lower-bound problem for tropical circuits, linking shortest paths, pure dynamic programming, and provenance computation. The gap concerns a basic polynomial-time task rather than a specialized graph family.

progress.text: Jukna gives the \(O(n^{3}) \min\)-plus upper bound and explicitly asks for a cubic lower bound for the single-pair connectivity polynomial; his framework distinguishes nonnegative tropical evaluation from formal polynomial production.

The author’s book supplements discuss the known cubic all-pairs lower bound and the unresolved single-source and single-pair optimality questions. The all-pairs argument does not directly settle one output.

Koutris restates the question for complete undirected graphs over absorptive semirings, recording the \(O(n^{3})\) upper bound and the quadratic input-dependence lower bound, with the gap open already over the tropical semiring.

context_blocks.text: The numerical task is elementary to state: return one shortest-path distance. The difficulty is understanding what can be done by a fixed network of minimum and addition operations. An algorithm that chooses which vertex to process next using comparisons may use information to control its future computation. This circuit model cannot turn the identity of a minimum into arbitrary control flow. Consequently, a fast implementation of a graph-search algorithm does not automatically supply a circuit of comparable size.

A concrete upper bound comes from repeated relaxation. Initialize \(d_{0}(1)=0\) and \(d_{0}(v)\)=infinity otherwise, and compute \(d_{k}(v)=\min\)(\(d_{k-1}(v), \min\) over u distinct from v of \(d_{k-1}(u)+x_{uv}\)). After n-1 layers, output \(d_{n-1}(n)\). Each layer uses \(O(n^{2})\) gates. Nonnegative weights ensure that deleting cycles cannot increase a walk’s cost, so these layers suffice for the simple-path optimum. This gives \(O(n^{3})\) gates.

Every edge can influence the answer: choose a simple source-to-target path through that edge, make its other edges cheap, and all edges outside the path expensive. Thus dependence on the quadratic number of inputs gives a quadratic lower bound, but does not charge separately for repeated reuse of intermediate computations. The missing factor n is the substantive issue.

For all-pairs shortest paths, a cubic lower bound is known in the same general min-plus framework. Its many required outputs are essential to the usual argument; requesting only the distance from 1 to n leaves room for different sharing. The database formulation places the question in absorptive semirings, where adding an unnecessary detour is absorbed. This card fixes the nonnegative tropical instance so that its allowed operations and output are unambiguous.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for integer multiplication
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(n_{0}\ge 1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}, a\) Boolean circuit of at most Cn gates maps every pair of n-bit unsigned integers to all 2n bits of their exact product?
cards.definitions: The circuit has input bits \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{n- 1},b_{0},\ldots ,b_{n- 1}\), representing \(a=\sum_{i}a_{i}2^{i}\) and \(b=\sum_{i}b_{i}2^{i}\), and output bits \(c_{0},\ldots ,c_{2n- 1}\) satisfying \(\sum_{j}c_{j}2\)ʲ=ab. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; constants 0 and 1 are allowed. Size counts gates, excluding input nodes and output wires. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. There is one circuit for each n, with no uniformity requirement on how these circuits are generated. Every input must be answered exactly, with no randomness. Leading zeros are permitted. Let \(M(n)\) be the minimum gate count in this model; the proposition is \(M(n)=O(n)\). Changing to any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes size by only a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified linear-size upper bound, or prove its negation: for every C and every \(n_{0}\) there is \(n\ge n_{0}\) with \(M(n)>Cn\). A lower bound \(c\cdot n\) with fixed c, a lower bound for bounded depth or restricted wiring, or a limitation of a particular multiplication algorithm does not give the required negative answer. A uniform linear-bit-time algorithm would imply the upper bound, but is a stronger demand than the existence of these nonuniform circuits.

context_blocks.text: Addition admits circuits whose gate count grows linearly with the input width. Multiplication is another elementary arithmetic operation, but the corresponding linear-size bound remains unknown. Goldreich singles it out immediately after the general challenge of proving a superlinear Boolean-circuit lower bound for an explicit function.

The circuit computes every output bit, including carries and the most significant half of the product. Treating a multiplication instruction on a whole machine word as one operation would hide the work being measured. The target concerns exact Boolean computation at individual-bit granularity.

Viola’s author manuscript, carrying a 2023–2026 revision notice, explicitly retains the linear-size multiplication question in Section 4.2. It also proves that multiplication and squaring are equivalent for this linear-size threshold: multiplication gives squaring immediately, and the converse uses squares together with linear-size addition and subtraction.

A negative answer would give a superlinear lower bound for a particularly concrete, efficiently computable family of multi-output Boolean functions. It would apply even to circuits tailored separately to each input length. A positive answer would show that the familiar logarithmic overhead of fast multiplication constructions is not necessary in this circuit model.

The existing TCS-7174 asks for optimal time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine. This card asks only about nonuniform gate count. The archived Karatsuba entry TCS-5168 concerns a reversible pebbling tradeoff, and TCS-6494 asks for a particular reduction from matrix transposition; neither is this unrestricted linear-size question.

cards.title: Optimal multilinear-formula size of the permanent
cards.formal: Determine the growth of \(\log _{2} F(n)\) up to universal multiplicative constants as \(n\to \infty\), where \(F(n)\) is the minimum size of a multilinear arithmetic formula over \(\mathbb{C}\) computing \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}\). Equivalently, find a positive function \(g(n)\) and constants \(a,A>0,n_{0}\) such that \(2^{a g(n)}\le F(n)\le 2^{A g(n)}\) for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\).
cards.definitions: The permanent is \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}(X)=\sum_{\pi \in S_{n}}\prod _{i=1}^{n} x_{i,\pi (i)}\). An arithmetic formula is a finite rooted tree with variable or complex-constant leaves and binary addition or multiplication gates, evaluated as a commutative polynomial. Every gate must compute a multilinear polynomial: every variable has degree at most one in every monomial after cancellation. The formula must agree identically with \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}\) on \(\mathbb{C} ^{n^{2}}\), not merely on Boolean inputs. Size counts all gates, including leaves. No restriction on the numerical complexity of complex constants is imposed. Let \(F(n)\) be the minimum such size; it is attained because sizes are positive integers and the defining sum of monomials is a valid finite multilinear formula. The independent variables are the \(n^{2}\) entries of the matrix; n denotes its row count. Internal computations are required to be multilinear as polynomials after cancellation, not just at the output. Sharing of subexpressions is forbidden by the tree model. The requested precision is constant factors in \(\log _{2} F(n)\), not constant factors in \(F(n)\).

cards.title: Semantic versus syntactic multilinear circuits
cards.formal: Is there a field \(F\), fixed independently of \(n\), and a family \(f_n\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \(n\ge1\), that has polynomial-size semantically multilinear arithmetic circuits over \(F\) but has no polynomial-size family of syntactically multilinear arithmetic circuits over that same field? Semantic multilinearity is required at every gate. The question uses nonuniform circuit size and allows arbitrary field constants.
cards.why: Many arithmetic lower bounds are proved under syntactic restrictions that make the variables entering a multiplication disjoint. Semantic multilinearity permits the same polynomial property to hold after cancellation and sharing of intermediate computations. Determining whether this distinction changes polynomial circuit power would clarify the scope of a central restricted model of algebraic computation.

cards.definitions: A field is a commutative field with \(0\ne1\); it may be finite or infinite and is chosen once for the entire family. An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output. Input gates are labelled by variables in \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) or by arbitrary elements of \(F\). Every internal gate has two input wires and is labelled \(+\) or \(\times\). Wires may reuse gate outputs, including as the two inputs of a gate, and both wires are then counted. Every gate lies on a path to the output. Size is one plus the number of wires; a field constant occupies one input gate irrespective of any representation length. There is no bound on depth or fan-out, no division gate, and no requirement that a circuit or its constants can be computed from \(n\). Each gate computes its formal polynomial in the polynomial ring \(F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). A polynomial is multilinear if every monomial with nonzero coefficient has exponent at most one in each variable; the zero polynomial is multilinear. A circuit is semantically multilinear if every gate computes such a polynomial, after all cancellations in \(F\). For each gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{Var}(g)\) be the set of variable labels occurring at input gates from which there is a directed path to \(g\), whether or not those variables cancel from its polynomial. A circuit is syntactically multilinear if \(\operatorname{Var}(g_1)\cap\operatorname{Var}(g_2)=\varnothing\) at every product gate with children \(g_1,g_2\). No such disjointness is required at addition gates. Let \(s_{\mathrm{sem},F}(f)\) and \(s_{\mathrm{syn},F}(f)\) be the minimum sizes of the respective circuits computing exactly \(f\). Equality means equality of formal polynomials, including over finite fields. Both minima are finite for a multilinear polynomial. Precisely, the target asks for \(F,(f_n)_{n\ge1},C>0,k\in\mathbb N\) such that \(\forall n\ge1,\ s_{\mathrm{sem},F}(f_n)\le C(n+1)^k\), while \(\forall B>0\;\forall d\in\mathbb N\;\forall N\ge1\;\exists n\ge N,\ s_{\mathrm{syn},F}(f_n)>B(n+1)^d\). Thus superpolynomial separation means failure of every polynomial bound for the family, with violations arbitrarily far out; an eventually exponential lower bound is not required. The field and family are existentially quantified before these asymptotic bounds.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated fixed-field family separation, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must establish polynomial semantic size and failure of every polynomial syntactic size bound for one family over one fixed field. A negative answer must show that over every field, each polynomial-size semantically multilinear family also has polynomial-size syntactically multilinear circuits, with polynomial constants allowed to depend on that field and family. No effective circuit-conversion algorithm is additionally required. A separation involving unrestricted intermediate polynomials, formulas only, bounded-depth circuits only or Boolean-function equality does not settle this comparison.

cards.title: Decidability of freeness in automaton groups
cards.formal: Is abstract freeness of an automaton group decidable? Does one deterministic Turing machine, given any finite complete deterministic invertible Mealy automaton \(\mathcal A\), always halt and return YES exactly when \[\exists r\in\mathbb N\quad G(\mathcal A)\cong F_r,\] where \(G(\mathcal A)\) is generated by all state transformations and their inverses and \(F_r\) is the free group of rank \(r\)? Rank zero, the trivial group, is included. The question does not require the supplied state transformations themselves to be a free basis.
cards.why: Automata give finite descriptions of groups that can have complex infinite structure and need not have finite presentations by relations. Recognizing a free group tests a fundamental structural property in this representation. The problem isolates the effect of invertibility on decidability and distinguishes structural recognition from equality of individual represented elements.

cards.definitions:
A finite complete deterministic Mealy automaton is \(\mathcal A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,\lambda)\), with finite nonempty state set \(Q\), finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and total tables \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\), \(\lambda:Q\times\Sigma\to\Sigma\). Invertibility means that for each state \(q\), the map \(a\mapsto\lambda(q,a)\) is a permutation of \(\Sigma\). No reversibility assumption is made on the maps \(q\mapsto\delta(q,a)\), and the numbers of states and letters are unbounded parts of the input. There are no designated initial or accepting states: all states are generators. The input is the full finite table, with binary state/letter indices and cardinalities. Invalid or noninvertible tables may be rejected.

The set \(\Sigma^*\) contains all finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Each state defines a transformation recursively by \(T_q(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\) and \(T_q(aw)=\lambda(q,a)T_{\delta(q,a)}(w)\). Invertibility makes each \(T_q\) a bijection of \(\Sigma^*\), preserving lengths and prefixes. The group \(G(\mathcal A)\) consists of all finite compositions of these functions and their inverses, including the empty composition, with function composition as multiplication. Equality means agreement on every finite input word of every length. This uses synchronous, total, one-letter-in/one-letter-out machines, rather than partial or asynchronous transducers.

The free group \(F_r\) has generators \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\) and their formal inverses. Its elements are finite reduced words, meaning adjacent inverse pairs have been cancelled; multiplication concatenates words and cancels such pairs, the empty word is the identity, and inversion reverses the word and flips each sign. Freeness of \(G(\mathcal A)\) means existence of a bijection to this group preserving multiplication and identity. A possible free basis may consist of arbitrary group elements rather than the given state list, which can contain identities, duplicates or dependent generators. Since the group is finitely generated, allowing all finite ranks is sufficient; no basis, rank, isomorphism or bound on relation length is supplied as an input promise or required as output.

The target is exact uniform decidability on every valid automaton table, with termination on both free and nonfree cases and no resource bound. One ordinary algorithm must work for all input sizes. No oracle, nonuniform advice, randomness, numerical tolerance or restriction to bounded input-word lengths is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that this predicate admits a total computable decider on the encoded complete invertible Mealy tables, or prove that it does not. The formalization must connect the state recursion, generated group of all-word transformations and existence of an abstract free-group isomorphism, including rank zero, to the algorithm's correctness and termination. A negative reduction must preserve complete deterministic invertibility. Deciding whether the named states freely generate, checking absence of a positive relation, or proving semigroup freeness undecidable does not by itself meet the abstract group target. Failure of one bounded relation search is not a proof that every total algorithm is impossible. The card review does not claim a verified Lean resolution.

The original 2000 list asks about the group’s structural properties, and the March 2026 handout defines freeness as isomorphism to a free group over some basis. This confirms that the target is not an injectivity test for the map from the free group on the names of all states.

For example, the usual adding machine generates an infinite cyclic group together with an identity state. The group is free of rank one, while the given state list is not a free basis and already contains a positive relation because the identity state acts trivially. Redundant state generators must therefore not force a NO answer.

cards.title: Sum-of-square-roots problem
cards.formal:
Does the sum-of-square-roots decision problem belong to deterministic polynomial time? An instance explicitly gives an integer \(n\ge1\), signed integers \(c_1,\ldots,c_n\), and positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), all in binary. The required answer is whether
\[
E(c,a)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i\sqrt{a_i}\ \ge0,
\]
where each square root is the nonnegative real square root. There is no promise that \(E\ne0\), that the radicands are distinct or square-free, or that their magnitudes are polynomial in \(n\). The target is one uniform deterministic algorithm with a polynomial bound in the total input bit length. This selects the standard algorithmic question explicitly stated in the newer sources; the original TOPP entry principally asks for tight separation bounds, a related quantitative question distinguished below.
cards.why: This is a basic barrier between exact geometric algorithms and computation on finite binary inputs. A general polynomial-time comparison procedure would remove a recurring obstacle to placing geometric decision and verification tasks in familiar discrete complexity classes. The problem also connects algebraic-number representation, exact numerical computation and the complexity of arithmetic circuits.
cards.status_note: The algorithmic question is explicitly open in the checked 2023–2024 primary sources. Individual source reading and a bounded later-work check through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution. This card selects polynomial-time exact comparison and explicitly distinguishes the original TOPP separation problem. The classification is a dated source-open assessment, not exhaustive proof verification or a claim that a Lean formalization already exists.

progress.text: The last listed TOPP revision records the separation problem and explicitly distinguishes a polynomial precision bound from the possibility of a polynomial-time sign algorithm.

Gaillard and Jindal distinguish the already polynomial-time equality problem for explicitly represented integers from generalized versions with arithmetic-program inputs. Their results for power series and succinct equality do not decide general sign comparison.

Balaji and Datta prove that the unary variant has polynomial-size circuit families, written \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\), in Theorem 1. Both the restricted magnitude regime and the allowed nonuniform advice differ from this card.

Eisenbrand, Haeberle and Singer explicitly state polynomial-time exact comparison as open. Theorem 6 improves separation as the integer coefficients vary while the radicands are fixed, with a non-explicit constant depending on those radicands.

Bläser, Dörfler and Jindal restate the signed-root decision problem and its relation to positivity of straight-line-program outputs. Their sum-of-squares results concern arithmetic-program problems and do not settle this decision problem.

sentences: The input describes a signed integer combination of square roots of positive integers using binary encodings.
The question is whether one deterministic algorithm can decide exactly whether its value is nonnegative in polynomial time.
All input magnitudes count toward the bit length, and zero or extremely small values are included.
The original separation-bound question, equality testing, unary inputs and nonuniform circuit results provide related context without settling this target.
A complete Lean proof must establish the uniform algorithm and its bound or prove that no such algorithm exists.

cards.definitions:
For \(a>0\), \(\sqrt a\) denotes the unique real \(r\ge0\) with \(r^2=a\). Coefficients may be positive, negative or zero, and repeated terms are permitted. The comparison is exact: when \(E=0\) the answer is yes, however close a nonzero \(E\) is to zero. No approximate value of \(E\), promise of a numerical gap or factorization of the radicands is supplied.

Fix the following binary encoding. For an integer \(r\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(r+1\); its code is \(\ell\) one-bits, one zero-bit and the \(\ell\)-bit binary expansion of \(r+1\). A signed integer \(c\) is encoded by the code of \(2c\) if \(c\ge0\), and of \(-2c-1\) otherwise. A valid instance is the code for \(n\ge1\), followed by the signed code for \(c_i\) and the code for \(a_i\ge1\), for each \(i=1,\ldots,n\) in order, with no trailing bits. Write \(L\) for the full encoded length. Define the language \(Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) to consist exactly of valid encodings for which \(E(c,a)\ge0\); every malformed string is outside \(Q\).

Computation uses a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes. Its fixed alphabet is \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), with \(\square\) blank. Tapes have nonnegative integer cell indices, all heads start at zero, and the input tape holds the input bits followed by blanks. One transition reads all scanned symbols, updates the state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; a left move at zero stays at zero. Two halting states output zero and one. Each transition costs one, including all parsing and arithmetic work. The program and number of tapes are independent of the instance. There is no advice, randomness, oracle, exact-real register or unit-cost square-root instruction.

The statement \(Q\in\mathrm P\) means
\[
\exists M\ \exists C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists d\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\
\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*}:
\]
the single machine \(M\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) transitions and outputs one exactly when \(x\in Q\). Thus the clock holds on every binary input, and all binary magnitudes contribute to the measured length. No running-time dependence exponential in \(n\), in the largest radicand or in its bit length is hidden in the polynomial constants.
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(Q\in\mathrm P\), or that \(Q\notin\mathrm P\), for the stated encoding and machine model. A positive answer must provide the one finite machine and polynomial constants and prove termination, the uniform time bound and both correctness directions on all inputs. A negative answer must show that for every such machine \(M\) and every \(C\ge1,d\ge0\), some binary input either is not answered within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) transitions or is answered incorrectly.

A proof for equality testing alone, unary inputs, a fixed number of terms, inputs separated from zero by a promised gap, or a unit-cost real-arithmetic model does not meet the criterion. Nor does a lower bound against a particular numerical procedure prove the negative answer. This is an unconditional yes/no complexity question: a conditional separation of complexity classes or a merely conditional algorithm does not decide it.

context_blocks.text: Euclidean distances between points with integer coordinates are square roots of integers. Comparing the lengths of two routes therefore leads to sums of these quantities. Binary input represents the integers compactly, while the comparison may depend on a very small difference between real numbers. Exact equality is part of the problem, rather than an excluded case.

TOPP Problem 33 primarily asks for tight upper and lower bounds on the minimum nonzero gap between two \(k\)-term square-root sums whose radicands are bounded by an integer \(B\). Its motivation asks whether the number of bits needed to separate the sums is polynomial in \(k\) and \(\log B\). This card explicitly chooses the standard polynomial-time decision question from the newer primary literature instead of presenting that separation problem as equivalent to it.

A sufficiently strong uniform separation bound would imply an efficient exact comparison algorithm. The converse is not asserted: TOPP explicitly allows that a polynomial-time comparison algorithm could exist even if its proposed precision bound fails. The algorithmic target places no requirement on how an algorithm represents its intermediate computation.

The signed-integer coefficient convention is the one used by Eisenbrand, Haeberle and Singer. The sign-list formulation in other references has the same polynomial-time decision status under polynomially related binary encodings. The card does not restrict to geometric instances, unary magnitudes or square-free radicands.

The 2024 separation theorem has a positive factor depending on the full tuple of radicands, without an explicit uniform bound on that dependence. Its improved dependence on the coefficients does not itself give a polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary binary instances. The unary result of Balaji and Datta instead supplies polynomial-size circuits, or polynomial-length advice depending on the input length; this is a different guarantee from one uniform algorithm.

Testing whether the sum is exactly zero is known to be polynomial-time decidable. Distinguishing a positive sum from a negative one remains the extra requirement. Recent work on succinct arithmetic-program encodings and on efficient practical exact comparison addresses other models or guarantees.

cards.title: Tensor orbit-closure intersection in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}\)
cards.formal:
Is the tensor orbit-closure intersection language \(L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\) defined below in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}\)? Equivalently, does it have both polynomially bounded certificates for yes-instances and a two-message public-coin Arthur–Merlin protocol for no-instances, with the completeness and soundness conditions below?

A valid input specifies positive integers \(n,m\) and two triples \(X=(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})\) and \(Y=(Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3})\) of \(nm\)-by-\(nm\) matrices with coefficients in \(\mathbb Q(i)\), given by their full lists of entries. On the ambient complex vector space
\[
\mathcal X_{n,m}=\bigl(\mathbb C^{nm\times nm}\bigr)^{\oplus3},
\]
the group \(G_{n,m}=\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb C)\) acts by
\[
(A,B)\cdot(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})=
\bigl((A\otimes B)X_{1}(A\otimes B)^{-1},
      (A\otimes B)X_{2}(A\otimes B)^{-1},
      (A\otimes B)X_{3}(A\otimes B)^{-1}\bigr).
\]
The input belongs to \(L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\) exactly when
\[
\overline{G_{n,m}\cdot X}^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}
\cap
\overline{G_{n,m}\cdot Y}^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}
\ne\varnothing.
\]
Invalid encodings do not belong to the language. Both dimensions and all coefficient bit lengths are unbounded parts of the input; the number of matrices in each triple is fixed at three. cards.definitions:
For a positive integer \(a\), write \([a]=\{1,\ldots,a\}\). Identify matrix rows and columns with \([n]\times[m]\) in lexicographic order. The Kronecker product is specified by
\[
(A\otimes B)_{(u,v),(u',v')}=A_{u,u'}B_{v,v'}.
\]
The same pair \((A,B)\) acts on all three matrices in a triple. Here \(\mathrm{GL}_{a}(\mathbb C)\) is the group of all invertible \(a\)-by-\(a\) complex matrices; its elements are not restricted to rational entries, determinant one, or unitary matrices. The inverse in the action is the ordinary matrix inverse, not a conjugate transpose. The input matrices need not be Hermitian, positive, normalized or invertible. This matrix representation identifies \(\mathcal X_{n,m}\) with
\[
\bigl(V\otimes V^{*}\otimes W\otimes W^{*}\bigr)^{\oplus3},
\qquad V=\mathbb C^{n},\quad W=\mathbb C^{m},
\]
where the stars denote complex-linear dual spaces, on which the group acts by the inverse dual action.

For a subset \(S\subseteq\mathcal X_{n,m}\), its Zariski closure is
\[
\overline S^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}
=\{z\in\mathcal X_{n,m}:\ \forall p\in\mathbb C[\mathcal X_{n,m}],
\ ((\forall s\in S,\ p(s)=0)\Longrightarrow p(z)=0)\},
\]
where \(\mathbb C[\mathcal X_{n,m}]\) is the ring of polynomials with complex coefficients in the \(3n^{2}m^{2}\) matrix-entry coordinates. The orbit is \(G_{n,m}\cdot X=\{g\cdot X:g\in G_{n,m}\}\). In this setting the Zariski and Euclidean closures of each orbit coincide. The decision predicate concerns intersection of the two closures, not equality of the original orbits, containment of one orbit closure in the other, or a positive-distance approximation promise. A point in the intersection may have arbitrary complex coordinates and is not supplied with the input.

The coefficient field for the finite input is fixed as \(\mathbb Q(i)=\{a+ib:a,b\in\mathbb Q\}\), embedded in \(\mathbb C\) with \(i^{2}=-1\). Write each coefficient uniquely as \(p/q+i\,r/s\), where \(p,r\in\mathbb Z\), \(q,s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), \(\gcd(|p|,q)=\gcd(|r|,s)=1\). Thus a zero real or imaginary part has denominator one. An unsigned integer is its usual binary expansion with no leading zeros, with zero written 0. A signed integer is a sign symbol, \(+\) or \(-\), followed by the unsigned expansion of its absolute value; the sign of zero is always \(+\).

To encode an instance, form a list of tokens: first \(1^{n}\), then \(1^{m}\), then the tokens \(p,q,r,s\) for every coefficient of \(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3}\), in that order and with each matrix listed in row order. Numerators use the signed format and denominators the unsigned format. Place the separator \(\#\) between consecutive tokens and no separator at either end. Turn this five-symbol string into binary using
\[
0\mapsto000,\quad1\mapsto001,\quad\#\mapsto010,
\quad+\mapsto011,\quad-\mapsto100.
\]
All other binary strings are invalid, including strings with the wrong number of entries, invalid dimensions, noncanonical fractions or unused three-bit codes. Let \(t=|z|\) be the complete bit length of an input string \(z\). Both unary dimension tokens and every sign, numerator and denominator bit count toward \(t\). This fixes an exact language on \(\{0,1\}^{*}\); it does not use a real-arithmetic oracle or a succinct tensor representation.

A deterministic verifier is one multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes, and the indicated read-only input tapes. A transition reads and writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell, and counts as one step. Inputs start between end markers; the machine returns a single accept/reject bit. There is no advice, oracle, uncharged preprocessing, or unit-cost operation on arbitrarily long integers or complex numbers. The machines, polynomial length bounds and time bounds are fixed before the input \(z\), and all running-time guarantees are worst-case bounds. Every polynomial length or time function below has fixed nonnegative integer coefficients; time bounds are positive. Such bounds may be enlarged by polynomial padding without changing the classes.

The assertion \(L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\in\mathrm{NP}\) means that there exist a deterministic verifier \(V_{N}\), a polynomial certificate-length function \(a:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), and a polynomial time bound \(T_{N}\), such that, for every input string \(z\) of length \(t\), the verifier halts within \(T_{N}(t)\) steps on every auxiliary string \(w\in\{0,1\}^{a(t)}\), and
\[
z\in L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{a(t)},\ V_{N}(z,w)=1.
\]
Thus every yes-instance has some accepting certificate, and no certificate is accepted on a no-instance.

The assertion \(L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\in\mathrm{coAM}\) means that its complement has the following Arthur–Merlin protocol. There exist a deterministic verifier \(V_{A}\), polynomial functions \(b,c:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), and a polynomial time bound \(T_{A}\). On input \(z\) of length \(t\), Arthur samples \(r\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^{b(t)}\) using independent fair bits and sends the entire string to Merlin. After seeing \(z,r\), Merlin returns an arbitrary string \(w\in\{0,1\}^{c(t)}\), and Arthur accepts exactly when \(V_{A}(z,r,w)=1\). Merlin has no computational restriction. The verifier must halt within \(T_{A}(t)\) steps on every such \(z,r,w\). Define the maximum acceptance probability
\[
\alpha(z)=2^{-b(t)}
\left|\left\{r\in\{0,1\}^{b(t)}:
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{c(t)},\ V_{A}(z,r,w)=1\right\}\right|.
\]
The required completeness and soundness inequalities are
\[
z\notin L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\Longrightarrow\alpha(z)\ge\frac{2}{3},
\qquad
z\in L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\Longrightarrow\alpha(z)\le\frac{1}{3}.
\]
The existential response is inside the probability over Arthur’s message because Merlin sees that message. There is no input distribution and no restriction to generic tensors. The randomness belongs only to Arthur; an auxiliary witness need not encode an algebraic transformation or a common limit.

For the class-level wording, a polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(A\) to a language \(B\) is a single deterministic polynomial-time map \(f\) on binary strings such that \(z\in A\) if and only if \(f(z)\in B\). The source proves that the double-conjugation problem above is complete for the tensor orbit-closure intersection class \(\mathrm{TOCI}\), with the input coefficient field fixed to \(\mathbb Q(i)\). Thus \(\mathrm{TOCI}\) can equivalently be defined here as all languages polynomial-time many-one reducible to \(L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\). Since \(\mathrm{NP}\) and \(\mathrm{coAM}\) are closed under these reductions, the target is equivalent to \(\mathrm{TOCI}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}\) for this fixed coefficient field.
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of
\[
L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\in\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}
\]
or of its negation for the exact input language, complex group action and bit model specified above.

A positive answer supplies the two uniform verifier machines and their polynomial bounds, proves the deterministic certificate equivalence for every binary input, and proves the public-coin protocol’s completeness and soundness inequalities for every binary input and every allowed prover response. The relevant existential choices of machines and polynomials must precede the universal quantifier over the input. Certificates and messages can be arbitrary binary strings of the specified lengths; no additional semantic form is required.

A negative answer proves
\[
L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\notin\mathrm{NP}\quad\lor\quad
L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\notin\mathrm{coAM}.
\]
Here each nonmembership assertion is the negation of the full verifier-and-polynomial existence statement in the definitions, so it excludes every eligible verifier with every polynomial choice, rather than just a particular certificate format or algorithm. A conditional nonmembership result under an unproved assumption does not settle this unconditional question. Membership in just one of the two classes, a special dimension regime, an average-case result, or a protocol with unspecified bit lengths and running time is insufficient. This is a class-membership proposition, so no additive numerical tolerance applies.

cards.formal: Assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, is approximate polynomial satisfiability for rational-coefficient arithmetic circuits in AM? An instance consists of division-free circuits computing \(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{m}\in \mathbb{Q} [x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\). It is a YES instance if, for every real \(\eta >0\), there is a point \(a\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\) with \(\max _{i} |f_{i}(a)|<\eta\); otherwise it is a NO instance. Equivalently, for every polynomial \(A\in \mathbb{Q} [y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m}]\), the identity \(A(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{m})=0\) must imply \(A(0,\ldots ,0)=0\). cards.definitions:
The integers n,m are positive and part of the instance. Each circuit is a finite acyclic graph with input gates \(x_{j}\) or rational constants and binary +,−,× gates; no division by expressions is allowed. The encoding lists gates in topological order, their input indices, their types, and the output gates. A rational constant is given by signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. The bit length L counts this entire finite description, including constants and gate references. Variables can be relabeled so n is at most the description length; unused variables do not affect the predicate. Shared gates are allowed. Neither total degree nor the magnitudes of intermediate coefficients are promised polynomial in L. The target is a Turing bit-complexity bound, not unit-cost arithmetic with arbitrary complex constants.

An annihilator is a nonzero polynomial \(A(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\) such that substituting the \(f_{i}\) yields the zero polynomial. Equivalently one can quantify over all A, including zero as in the formal statement. AnnAtZero asks whether every such A has zero constant term, not whether some annihilator exists. In particular, algebraically independent \(f_{i}\) satisfy it vacuously. The same condition holds if the annihilator coefficients are allowed in the algebraic closure \(\bar\{\mathbb{Q}\}\). A further equivalent algebraic formulation is: there are finite Laurent polynomials \(\beta _{j}(t)\in \bar\{\mathbb{Q}\}[t,t^{- 1}]\) such that \(f_{i}(\beta _{1}(t),\ldots ,\beta _{n}(t))\in t\bar\{\mathbb{Q}\}[t]\) for every i. Negative powers in the \(\beta _{j}\) are permitted, but all nonpositive powers must disappear after evaluation of each \(f_{i}\). There is no input error tolerance or promised bound on the exponents, coefficient descriptions or sizes of these witnesses. The Laurent formulation is equivalent to the rational-function formulation in the source. Geometrically, the origin belongs to the Zariski closure of the polynomial image \(f(\mathbb{C} ^{n})\): the smallest set defined by polynomial equations containing that image. For complex polynomial maps this is also equivalent to membership in its Euclidean closure, giving the \(\eta\) formulation. The approximating points may escape every bounded region; the target does not require an exact common zero in \(\mathbb{C} ^{n}\).

AM means the following. There are a deterministic polynomial-time bit algorithm V and polynomials r,p such that Arthur samples a uniformly random string \(u\in \{0,1\}^{r(\mathrm{L})}\) and sends it to Merlin, who returns \(w\in \{0,1\}^{p(\mathrm{L})}\); then V(instance,u,w) accepts or rejects. Merlin knows the instance and u and has unlimited computation. All verifier randomness is in u; the verifier has no remaining private coins. For every YES instance, \(\Pr _{u}\)[\(\exists w:V\)(instance,u,w)=1]\(\ge 2/3\), and for every NO instance this probability is at most \(1/3\). Constants and polynomial exponents are universal across n,m,L. Shorter messages may be padded. GRH here is the usual number-field form: every nontrivial zero in \(0<Re(s)<1\) of the Dedekind zeta function \(\zeta _{K}(s)\) of every number field K has real part \(1/2\). It is an assumption, not an oracle supplied to the verifier. The task asks for the stated inclusion under that assumption; no certificate of the truth of GRH is demanded.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove, under GRH, that one AM protocol satisfying the stated bounds decides every encoded instance, or refute the inclusion under the same assumption. A protocol only for exact common-root existence, algebraic dependence, bounded-degree special cases, or finite fields does not establish the target. A PSPACE algorithm or a test at one fixed positive numerical tolerance is insufficient. Failure of a proposed protocol is not a proof that APS is outside AM.

cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic \(O(n)\)-time algorithm which, given two permutations \(\pi,\tau\) of \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), returns a permutation \(\rho\) satisfying \(A_\rho(i,j)=\min_{0\le h\le n}(A_\pi(i,h)+A_\tau(h,j))\) for all \(0\le i,j\le n\)?

For a permutation \(
u\), define \(A_
u(i,j)=|\{t:i\le t<n,\ 
u(t)<j\}|\). This counting matrix is the implicit simple unit-Monge representation used here. The input is the two permutation arrays, and the output is the array \(ho\); no \((n+1)\)-by-\((n+1)\) matrix is supplied or requested explicitly. cards.title: Polynomial-time computation of addition-chain length
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(K>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) and one deterministic multitape Turing machine that, on every positive integer \(n\) supplied in binary, outputs the exact shortest addition-chain length \(\ell(n)\) in binary within \(K(b+1)^a\) steps, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\) is the input length?
cards.definitions:
An addition chain for \(n\ge1\) is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers
\[
1=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_r=n
\]
such that for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there exist indices \(j,k\in\{0,\ldots,i-1\}\) with \(a_i=a_j+a_k\). The two indices may coincide, and an earlier entry may be reused any number of times. The length is the number \(r\) of additions, not the number \(r+1\) of entries. Define \(\ell(n)\) as the minimum such length; in particular, \(\ell(1)=0\). The only initially available number is \(1\). Subtraction, division, multiplication of chain entries and additional initial constants are not chain operations. The sum need not use the immediately preceding entry.

The machine receives just the ordinary binary expansion of \(n\), with no leading zeros. Its output is the ordinary binary expansion of the integer \(\ell(n)\), with \(0\) written as a single zero bit. The same finite program and constants must work for all valid inputs. The program has the usual unrestricted finite alphabet and binary work tapes of a multitape Turing machine, but all work, input reads and output writing count in its worst-case step bound. It has no advice, oracle, random bits or uncharged preprocessing. Invalid input strings must be rejected within the same bound with \(b\) interpreted as their string length. No addition chain or auxiliary number-theoretic data are supplied.

The requested machine may use any deterministic computation to find the length; the restrictions on chain operations define the quantity being optimized, rather than restricting the machine's internal calculations. The output is only the optimal length, not a chain attaining it. The input is a single binary target, not a list of targets and not a unary string of length \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm and fixed polynomial bound satisfying the exact-output task for every \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. Exact integer output is part of this computational existence question, not an extra accuracy restriction on a numerical-value benchmark. A fast approximation, a heuristic, polynomial time in \(n\) instead of its bit length, or a result for special targets does not meet the stated guarantee. Conditional hardness must retain its assumption; hardness of forming several prescribed targets is a different problem.

cards.definitions:
Write \(q=p^e\), where \(p\ge2\) is prime and \(e\ge1\). The field is supplied as \(\mathbb F_p[X]/(h(X))\), with a monic irreducible polynomial \(h(X)=X^e+\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}h_jX^j\) over \(\mathbb F_p\). Its elements are the coefficient vectors of representatives of degree less than \(e\), with coefficients in \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\); addition and multiplication mean polynomial addition and multiplication modulo \(p\) and \(h\). Primality and irreducibility are promises, not extra input-search tasks. Fix the following bit encoding. Give \(n,d,e\) as three unary strings terminated by zero, then the bit length \(\ell\) of \(p\) in unary terminated by zero, then the \(\ell\)-bit ordinary binary expansion of \(p\). Give \(h_0,\ldots,h_{e-1}\), followed by the entries of \(A_1,\ldots,A_d\) in matrix order and row-major order, each residue coefficient as an \(\ell\)-bit unsigned block. Matrix entries use their \(e\) coefficients in increasing degree. Let \(L\) be the length of this complete representation. All arithmetic cost is bit cost; field operations are not free unit-cost oracle calls.

A subspace \(V\) is any linear subspace over this supplied field, not merely the span of a subset of coordinate vectors. \(A_iV=\{A_iv:v\in V\}\), and the sum \(A_1V+\cdots+A_dV\) is their linear span, not a union or the intersection of their images. All dimensions are over \(\mathbb F_q\). The range \(1\le\dim V\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) is nonempty because \(n\ge2\); the finite field makes the minimum range finite. Each candidate ratio has numerator between zero and \(n\) and denominator between one and \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Hence the output has a polynomial-length exact representation as a reduced nonnegative fraction with positive denominator, both in binary. No subspace attaining the minimum needs to be output. The original subspace is not automatically added to its image: \(V+\sum_iA_iV\) would be a different quantity unless an identity map were included. Matrices need not be invertible, contain the identity, be distinct, or already form an expander. The value can be below one, including zero; in that case the tuple meets none of the source’s expander conditions requiring an expansion factor at least one.

The algorithm is a single finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machine, with no advice, random bits or external oracles. Ask for constants \(C,c\ge1\) independent of \(p,e,n,d,h,A_i\) such that it halts on every valid promised input, returns the exact specified fraction and uses at most \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions, including preprocessing, field arithmetic and output. No claim for characteristic-zero fields or a black-box field representation is included.

cards.title: Explicit univariate arithmetic circuit lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a family \(f=(f_d)_{d\ge2}\in\mathcal E\) whose arithmetic circuit complexity over \(\mathbb C\) is not \(O(\log d)\)? Precisely, \[\exists f\in\mathcal E\ \forall K\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall D\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\ \exists d\in\mathbb N,\ d\ge D:\ S_{\mathbb C}(f_d)>K\log_2 d.\] Every \(f_d\in\mathbb Z[x]\) has degree exactly \(d\); \(\mathcal E\) is the class with the uniform coefficient-bit algorithm and polynomial coefficient-length bound defined below. Circuits are unrestricted binary addition/multiplication circuits with arbitrary complex constants, and \(S_{\mathbb C}\) counts wires. This is a disclosed editorial specialization of Wigderson's Open Problem 12.1: it retains the not-\(O(\log d)\) threshold, selects the complex field permitted by the source, and makes explicitness precise using ITCS 2021 Definition 1.
cards.why: This target asks whether efficiently accessible integer coefficients force unrestricted arithmetic computation beyond the elementary logarithmic degree bound, even with one variable and arbitrary complex constants. sentences: The question asks for a family of one-variable integer polynomials whose smallest arithmetic circuits cannot all be bounded by a constant times the logarithm of their degree.
Each polynomial must have polynomially many bits per coefficient, with any requested coefficient bit and sign computable by one uniform algorithm in time polynomial in the logarithm of the degree.
The competing circuits may share intermediate computations and use arbitrary complex constants for free, while every wire into a binary addition or multiplication gate contributes to their size.
This explicitness requirement is a disclosed specialization of the original question, whose wording did not fix a coefficient-generation model.
A resolution would clarify how far efficiently specified coefficients can force arithmetic complexity beyond the elementary degree bound in a single variable.

cards.definitions:
The index \(d\) ranges over all integers at least two. Write
\[f_d(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_{d,i}x^i,\qquad a_{d,i}\in\mathbb Z,\quad a_{d,d}\ne0.\]
Integer coefficients are embedded in \(\mathbb C\) in the usual way. All identities are exact formal polynomial identities in \(\mathbb C[x]\).

An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output. Input nodes are labeled by \(x\) or arbitrary elements of \(\mathbb C\). Every other node has two operand slots and is labeled \(+\) or \(\times\), computing the sum or product of its operand polynomials. The operands may coincide, in which case both wires are counted. Intermediate results may be reused arbitrarily often. Only nodes used by the output are retained. Size is the total number of wires, equivalently twice the number of binary arithmetic gates. Define \(S_{\mathbb C}(g)\) as the minimum size of such a circuit computing \(g\); every polynomial has a finite circuit, so this minimum exists.

Constant labels may depend on \(d\) and the circuit, with no restriction on magnitude, computability or binary length and no cost for constructing them. Their uses as operands contribute wires. There are no division, primitive power, comparison, branch, bit-extraction or coefficient-query gates. Negative constants permit subtraction to be expressed with the allowed operations. Depth, fan-out, intermediate degrees and intermediate coefficients are unrestricted; cancellation is permitted. Circuits are nonuniform: they may be chosen separately at each degree, without an algorithm constructing the sequence.

For \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(q\in\mathbb N\), define
\[\mathrm{query}(a,q)=\begin{cases}1,&q=0\text{ and }a<0,\\0,&q=0\text{ and }a\ge0,\\\lfloor |a|/2^{q-1}\rfloor\bmod2,&q\ge1.\end{cases}\]
Thus query zero is the sign bit, and queries \(1,2,\ldots\) give magnitude bits starting with the least significant bit. Zero has sign zero, and leading magnitude bits are zero.

The family belongs to \(\mathcal E\) if there exist fixed integers \(B,A,k\ge1\) and one deterministic finite-program Turing machine \(M\) such that, for all \(d\ge2\) and \(0\le i\le d\),
\[|a_{d,i}|<2^{d^B},\]
and, for every additional index \(0\le q\le d^B\), \(M\) on input \(\mathrm{bin}(d)\#\mathrm{bin}(i)\#\mathrm{bin}(q)\) outputs exactly \(\mathrm{query}(a_{d,i},q)\) within
\[A(1+\lceil\log_2 d\rceil)^k\]
steps. Binary representations have no leading zeroes, with zero represented by \(0\); \(\#\) is a separator. The coefficient bound permits at most \(d^B\) magnitude bits, and this query range includes them all and the sign. Every valid input therefore has length \(O_B(\log d)\). The same machine and constants work for every degree and query. They may depend on the family.

Here \(M\) is an ordinary deterministic multitape bit Turing machine: it has a fixed finite alphabet, a fixed finite number of work tapes initially blank and a read-only input tape; each transition reads and updates only the symbols under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell. Output is charged. No randomization, advice, oracle, unbounded-precision primitive or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. No behavior is required outside the stated valid query domain. Any fixed standard Turing-machine convention yields the same class because arbitrary fixed polynomial time bounds are allowed.

The explicitness requirement gives access to individual coefficient bits; it does not require printing whole coefficients or the entire coefficient list in time polynomial in \(\log d\). This bit-computation algorithm is separate from the complex arithmetic circuits whose size is measured. The target says that \(S_{\mathbb C}(f_d)/\log_2 d\) is unbounded on every tail, not that it tends to infinity at all sufficiently large degrees.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence statement or its full logical negation \[\forall f\in\mathcal E\ \exists K\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists D\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\ \forall d\ge D:\ S_{\mathbb C}(f_d)\le K\log_2 d.\] A positive answer must specify one family, its coefficient-query machine and constants \(B,A,k\), prove exact degree \(d\), coefficient lengths, and query correctness and running time, and prove the lower-bound quantifiers against all allowed complex-constant circuits. A negative answer must cover every family in \(\mathcal E\); its \(K,D\) may depend on the family, and its small circuits may vary nonuniformly with \(d\). Showing that one proposed family has small circuits does not refute this existential target. Mere nonconstructive existence, a lower bound only for restricted constants, formulas, bounded depth, monotone or noncommutative circuits, or a weighted sum-of-squares bound alone is insufficient. The target retains not-\(O(\log d)\), without demanding a stronger superpolylogarithmic or almost-everywhere bound. An implication from an additional unproved complexity assumption is conditional progress rather than an unconditional resolution.

cards.title: VP factor closure in positive characteristic
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{VP}_{F}\) closed under polynomial factors for every field \(F\) of positive characteristic? Explicitly, quantify first over every prime \(p\), every field \(F\) with \(\operatorname{char}(F)=p\), every function \(m:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N\), and every two polynomial families
\[
f_n,g_n\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\qquad(n\ge1).
\]
Does the following implication always hold?
\[
\begin{split}
&\left[\ \forall n\ge1,\ f_n\ne0\text{ and }g_n\mid f_n\ \right]\\
&\quad\land\left[\ \exists A,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,\
\max\{m(n),\deg(f_n),L_F(f_n)\}\le A(n+1)^k\ \right]\\
&\qquad\Longrightarrow\left[\ \exists B,\ell\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,\
L_F(g_n)\le B(n+1)^{\ell}\ \right]?
\end{split}
\]
Here \(L_F\) is exact algebraic circuit size as defined below, and degree means total degree. The field is fixed throughout each family. Constants in the polynomial bounds may depend on the field and the families but not on \(n\). There is no restriction on factor multiplicities, including multiplicities divisible by \(p\).
cards.why: Factor closure asks whether multiplication can conceal a polynomial that is substantially harder to compute than the resulting product, even when all output degrees remain polynomially bounded. It is a structural question about the standard class of efficiently computable polynomial families. Its positive-characteristic form is also relevant to the scope of algebraic hardness-versus-randomness results, where extracting factors from circuit identities connects lower bounds with polynomial identity testing.
cards.status_note: The original Question 3 remains explicitly open as Open Problem 4.4.1 in the survey revision accepted 12 June 2026. Checked finite-field VNP closure and recent small-characteristic factoring theorems do not give the required VP circuits for the actual factors over the same arbitrary base field. Individual primary-source reading and bounded subsequent checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. This is a dated source-open assessment, not exhaustive verification of present-day openness or of all cited proofs.

progress.text: Andrews proves a circuit-size bound \(3sp^{2r}+2^r\) for extracting a \(p\)-th root from a size-\(s\) circuit on \(r\) variables, over the perfect closure of the base field. This is polynomial in \(s\) when \(r=O(\log_p s)\); it does not give polynomial overhead for unrestricted polynomially many variables.

Bhargav, Dwivedi and Saxena prove factor closure for \(\mathrm{VNP}\) over every finite field. Consequently, factors of \(\mathrm{VP}\) families over finite fields belong to \(\mathrm{VNP}\). This larger-class conclusion leaves the requested \(\mathrm{VP}\) closure unresolved.

Bhattacharjee and coauthors prove formula and bounded-depth circuit factor closure in characteristic zero. Their small-characteristic statement yields powers \(g^{p^{\ell}}\) of factors. A companion result places these powers over a sufficiently large base finite field, retaining the distinction between the power and the factor itself.
The revised Bhargav–Dwivedi–Saxena survey explicitly retains positive-characteristic \(\mathrm{VP}\) factor closure as Open Problem 4.4.1.

cards.definitions:
A field has characteristic \(p\) when \(p\) is the smallest positive integer such that the sum of \(p\) copies of \(1_F\) is zero. The statement includes finite and infinite fields, including fields that are not perfect or algebraically closed. A field of characteristic \(p\) is perfect if every element has a \(p\)-th root in that same field. This property is not an assumption of the question.

The variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}\) commute. Polynomial equality and divisibility are identities in the formal polynomial ring over \(F\), not equality only as functions on \(F^{m(n)}\). Thus \(g_n\mid f_n\) means that some \(h_n\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\) satisfies the identity \(f_n=g_nh_n\). The requirement \(f_n\ne0\) implies that both factors are nonzero. Constant factors and the whole polynomial are allowed. For a nonzero polynomial, total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient; nonzero constants have degree zero. The ring with zero variables is \(F\). Since \(F\) is a field and \(f_n\ne0\), a divisor has total degree at most \(\deg(f_n)\).

An algebraic circuit over \(F\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output gate. An input gate is labeled by a variable or by any element of \(F\). Every other gate has two ordered input positions, each referencing an earlier gate in a topological ordering, and is labeled by addition or multiplication. A predecessor may be used in both input positions. Fan-out is unrestricted, and the same intermediate polynomial may be reused. Evaluation is formal addition and multiplication in \(F[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\). The circuit size is the total number of gates, including variable and constant gates. The quantity \(L_F(u)\) is the minimum such size among circuits computing \(u\) exactly.

No division, root-extraction, oracle or approximation gates are allowed. Arbitrary constants from the fixed base field each occupy one constant gate; their bit descriptions or computability are not charged. This is algebraic size complexity, not bit complexity. A circuit can equivalently be recorded as a topologically ordered finite list of gate labels and predecessor indices. The representation carries actual field elements as labels and is not required to encode them as finite binary strings. There is no restriction on circuit depth or on degrees of intermediate gates, and no randomness or permitted error in the circuit's output.

A family belongs to \(\mathrm{VP}_{F}\) when its number of variables, output total degree and minimum circuit size have polynomial bounds in the family index, precisely as in the antecedent. The circuits for distinct indices may be unrelated: neither the circuit family nor its field constants must be generated uniformly. The desired circuits for \(g_n\) are over the same \(F\), and may use any constants from \(F\). The target is the existence of a polynomial-size circuit family for every factor family. It does not request a deterministic or randomized algorithm producing those circuits from circuits for \(f_n\), a common exponent valid for every field and family, or a complete factorization as an algorithmic output.

For a nonconstant irreducible polynomial \(u\), its multiplicity in a nonzero polynomial \(f\) is the largest integer \(e\ge0\) for which \(u^e\mid f\). The question includes every choice of a divisor, with any collection of such multiplicities permitted by \(f_n\). No square-free, separability or multiplicity-coprime-to-characteristic promise is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed universal implication or of its negation. A positive answer must establish a polynomial bound for circuits computing the actual factor family over the same base field, for every admissible family and every field of positive characteristic. A negative answer must establish a fixed positive-characteristic field and admissible families with \((f_n)\in\mathrm{VP}_{F}\), \(g_n\mid f_n\) for every \(n\), and
\[
\forall B,\ell\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge1,\quad L_F(g_n)>B(n+1)^{\ell}.
\]
No efficient method for generating a counterexample family is additionally required. A bound only for a positive-characteristic power of the factor, a circuit over an extension field without a proved return to the base field, or membership in a larger class does not settle the question. A proof of the failure of one factoring algorithm is not a refutation of this nonuniform closure statement.

context_blocks.text: Kaltofen established the corresponding factor closure in characteristic zero. The source question asks whether this structural property of \(\mathrm{VP}\) persists without that characteristic restriction. Polynomial bounds on the original family’s output degree are part of the question; low-degree factors of circuits whose outputs have unbounded degree form a different, stronger factoring problem.

The source defines \(\mathrm{VP}\) as a nonuniform family class over a fixed field. This card expands that definition into explicit quantifiers. It makes the conventional exclusion of zero input polynomials and the requirement of formal polynomial identity explicit. Binary addition and multiplication gates fix a concrete size convention; the survey’s unrestricted-fan-in circuit convention gives the same polynomial-size class. These are declared modeling refinements, not a restriction to finite fields or a demand for a uniform factoring algorithm.

In characteristic \(p\), the identity \((a+b)^p=a^p+b^p\) creates a distinction between obtaining a small circuit for a factor and obtaining one for its \(p\)-power. Known positive-characteristic statements can retain such powers or enlarge the constant field. The present target requires the original factor over the original field, with arbitrary multiplicities.

cards.definitions: A sparse representation of f lists its nonzero rational coefficients and corresponding nonnegative integer exponent vectors; s is the number of listed monomials and d bounds the sum of exponents in each monomial. The candidate divisor g is supplied by its coefficients and exponent vectors; because \(\delta\) is fixed, it has at most \(binomial(n+\delta ,\delta )\) monomials, so dense and sparse explicit encodings are polynomially related. Divisibility means that a polynomial \(h\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) exists with \(f=gh\). The quotient need not be sparse and need not be output. The polynomial running-time exponent may depend on the fixed \(\delta\), but not on the input n,s,d. The source counts exact arithmetic operations over Q at unit cost. In particular, the requested bound is polynomial in the numerical degree d, not merely in log d, and is not a bound on rational-coefficient bit complexity. There is no promise that g is irreducible. The cases \(f=0\) or nonzero constant g have immediate affirmative answers; the first unsettled divisor degree is two.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic divisibility decision algorithm with the stated polynomial arithmetic cost for every fixed \(\delta\), or establish an obstruction to that precise guarantee. Randomized testing, quasipolynomial time, or a bound requiring the dividend f to have constant individual degree does not answer the question.
