cards.definitions: A polynomial family has \(f_{n}\in F[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{m(n)}]\), where \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_{n}\) are at most \(n^{a}+a\) for some fixed a. An algebraic formula is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are variables or constants in F and whose internal gates are binary addition or multiplication. Its output is a formal polynomial; equality means coefficientwise equality in \(F[x]\), also when F is finite. Its size is its number of nodes. An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated source and sink and affine-linear polynomial labels on edges. It computes the sum, over all source-to-sink paths, of the product of the labels on that path. Count vertices, edges and the nonzero coefficients used to describe edge labels as its size; these choices differ only polynomially from the usual size conventions. Field constants have unit algebraic cost, with no bit-length bound. \(VF_{F}\) and \(VBP_{F}\) consist respectively of the polynomial families with formula size and branching-program size bounded by \(n^{b}+b\) for some constant b independent of n. These are nonuniform classes: a different finite computation may be chosen for each n, with no requirement to generate it algorithmically. The separation asks for one family in \(VBP_{F}\) for which, for every b, some n requires formula size greater than \(n^{b}+b\). There is no restriction to multilinear computation, bounded depth, homogeneous intermediate gates or noncommuting variables.
cards.answer_criterion: For the stated field F, prove \(VF_{F} \subsetneq  VBP_{F}\) by exhibiting a family in \(VBP_{F}\) and proving that its formula sizes are not polynomially bounded, or prove \(VF_{F}=VBP_{F}\) by showing that every polynomial-size branching-program family has polynomial-size formulas. Any characteristic or field restriction must be stated as part of the scope of the answer. A lower bound only for bounded-depth or multilinear formulas does not resolve the unrestricted question.

cards.definitions: An algebraic circuit over \(\mathbb{C}\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with inputs \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\) and arbitrary complex constants, binary addition and multiplication gates, and one output. Subtraction is allowed via multiplication by −1; there are no division gates. Its size is its number of vertices. It computes an exact formal polynomial, and each constant is one field element regardless of its bit description. \(VP_{\mathbb{C}}\) consists of polynomial families with polynomially bounded total degree and polynomially bounded nonuniform algebraic circuit size. For \(d=n^{c}\), list all monomials \(x_{1}^{\alpha _{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\alpha _{n}}\) with \(\alpha _{i}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{i}\alpha _{i}\le d\) in a fixed lexicographic order of exponent vectors. There are \(N_{n}=\operatorname{binom}(n+d,n)\) such monomials. \(coeff(f)\) is the full vector of their coefficients, including zeros. \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is a polynomial over \(\mathbb{C}\) whose variables are these \(N_{n}\) coordinates. Nonzero means not the zero formal polynomial; over \(\mathbb{C}\) it is equivalent to being nonzero at some coefficient vector. Both degree and circuit size of \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) are bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(N_{n}\), not in n. The equations themselves are nonuniform: there is no additional requirement to construct their circuits in polynomial time from n. Vanishing must hold for all circuits under each fixed polynomial size bound eventually; the threshold can depend on that bound. Restricting c,b to positive integers covers arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents by increasing them. The statement imposes no bound on output coefficients of f or on constants used inside its circuit, and requests no explicit hard polynomial on which \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is nonzero.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of such a nontrivial polynomial-degree, polynomial-circuit-size family for every c, or refute the universal existence statement for at least one c. Vanishing only on polynomials with bounded integer coefficients, or only on a fixed restricted circuit architecture, does not establish the claim. Nonexistence of equations for VNP alone does not refute existence for VP.

cards.definitions:
A graph group, also called a right-angled Artin group, has one generator for every vertex in A. An edge specifies that its two generators commute. I is symmetric and has no loops. The displayed presentation imposes these commutation relations and the group axioms, with no additional relations such as a²=1. The alphabet A±1 contains each generator and a formal inverse. Products are identified under insertion or deletion of adjacent inverse pairs and interchange of adjacent commuting letters, including their inverses. The identity is the class of the empty word. For instance aba⁻¹b⁻¹ is the identity when a and b are joined by an edge; without that edge, it is nontrivial in the two-generator free group.

A straight-line program is an acyclic sequence of string assignments. In a convenient normal form, X_i is assigned an alphabet letter, the empty word, or a concatenation X_jX_k with j,k<i. A designated final variable produces val(S). Reusing a variable means reusing its whole generated string; it does not introduce a new unknown group element. General finite right-hand sides can be put in this form with polynomial overhead. The expanded string can have exponential length in the program size and is not given explicitly.

Vertices and variables have binary indices. The graph is given explicitly, for example by its vertex and edge lists, and every program instruction is listed explicitly. Let L be the total bit length of this representation. The requested bound is L^{O(1)} bit operations on a deterministic machine, with one exponent and one algorithm for the entire input family. It cannot hide an arbitrary dependence on |A| or the commutation graph in a supposedly fixed constant. Equivalent explicit encodings differing by polynomial factors give the same P-membership question. Ill-formed graphs or cyclic programs may be rejected in polynomial time.

For the weaker NP question, every identity instance would need a certificate of length polynomial in L verifiable deterministically in polynomial time; nonidentity instances must have no accepting certificate. The known coRP result instead gives a randomized polynomial-time identity test that always accepts identities and accepts any nonidentity with probability at most 1/3. This does not by itself put identity instances in NP. The target concerns an arbitrary compressed word, not merely a product u₁^{z₁}⋯u_t^{z_t} of explicitly written words with given binary integer exponents, and not the existence of unknown exponents.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove uniform deterministic polynomial-time decidability for arbitrary input commutation graphs and SLPs, or prove that no such algorithm exists, stating any complexity assumption used by a conditional obstruction. An NP upper bound is progress on the weaker branch and must not be reported as a positive answer to P-membership. A bound polynomial only for each fixed group, or an algorithm restricted to power words, does not settle this card.

cards.definitions:
Here \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). A sequence \(u\) is rationally recursive if there are an integer \(k\geq1\), rational initial values \(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\), and rational functions
\[F_{i}=P_{i}/Q_{i}\in\mathbb Q(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\qquad(1\leq i\leq k)\]
that generate a state sequence \(\mathbf z_{n}\in\mathbb Q^{k}\) by
\[\mathbf z_{0}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}),\qquad
z_{n+1,i}=F_{i}(\mathbf z_{n}),\qquad u_{n}=z_{n,1}.\]
All components are updated simultaneously from the preceding state. Each \(P_{i},Q_{i}\) is a finite polynomial with rational coefficients, \(Q_{i}\) is not the zero polynomial, and \(Q_{i}(\mathbf z_{n})\ne0\) for every \(i,n\). The other coordinates are auxiliary sequences.

The proposed scalar recurrence uses only the last \(d\) values of \(u\), in their stated order. Its coefficients are rational constants. It has no separate access to the index \(n\), the hidden coordinates, an externally supplied clock, or a rule that changes with \(n\). The first \(d\) actual values of \(u\) are its initial data.

The quantifiers permit \(d,A,B\) to depend on the entire sequence, including the original rational initial values. They must then work at every step. There is no requirement for one scalar recurrence to work uniformly for all initial vectors of a given mutual-update system, and no prescribed bound on \(d\), degree or coefficient size.

Denominators must be nonzero at every state or scalar window where the chosen fraction is evaluated. Algebraic cancellation may be used when choosing a fraction representation, but a recurrence is not allowed to evaluate \(0/0\), assign it an arbitrary value, or switch formulas to handle exceptional windows. The scalar recurrence must hold from \(n=0\), after its initial \(d\) values, rather than only on an unspecified eventual tail.

The claim is semantic existence of a finite recurrence over \(\mathbb Q\). It does not require an algorithm for finding one, a time bound for conversion, or an algorithm that checks whether an arbitrary proposed rational-update system avoids division by zero. The input class already consists of systems whose entire orbit is defined.

A scalar recurrence can always be expressed as a finite mutual system by retaining its finitely many preceding values as state. Thus the displayed direction is precisely the missing direction in the source’s equality of the two sequence classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed recurrence exists for every well-defined rationally recursive sequence over \(\mathbb Q\), or give such a sequence and prove that no finite \(d\) and no rational function with nonvanishing denominators along its windows can generate it in this way. A recurrence only for generic initial conditions, an implicit polynomial relation, or a rule with exceptional undefined evaluations does not settle the conjecture.
